title: The history of e-ink
tagline: From clay specks in a Moscow lab to a page that stays on screen with the power off, in two centuries.
intro: Charged specks moving in a liquid were noticed in 1807. It took until the 1970s to try them as a screen, and 1997 to seal them in capsules thin enough to print. A decade later a reader built on the idea sold to the public, and now the same ink can show colour.

eras.name: Specks in a field
eras.summary: Scientists see charged particles drift in water, and engineers wonder if that could make a picture.

eras.name: Electric paper
eras.summary: Two ideas compete: twisting balls at Xerox and ink in capsules at MIT. The capsules win.

eras.name: E-readers arrive
eras.summary: Sony, then Amazon, put e-ink in a book-sized device and people buy it.

eras.name: Light and colour
eras.summary: Frontlights, sharper screens and colour make e-paper work in more places.

events.title: Clay moves in an electric field
events.who: Ferdinand Frederic Reuss, with Peter Strakhov
events.text: At Moscow University, Ferdinand Reuss and Peter Strakhov saw clay grains in water drift when a steady electric current passed through it. Reuss published the result in 1809. Sources date the experiments to 1807, so the year is given as 1807, published 1809.
events.why: Moving charged particles with a field is the whole idea behind e-ink.

events.title: Patents for electrophoretic images
events.text: Isao Ota of Matsushita claimed Japanese priority dates of 23 April and 12 June 1969 for an "electrophoretic image reproduction process". It was later filed as a Canadian patent in 1970. A US patent for an electrophoretic display device by Ota followed that year.
events.why: Engineers were already trying to turn electrophoresis into a display.

events.title: Project Gutenberg digitises its first text
events.text: Michael Hart, a University of Illinois student, typed the US Declaration of Independence into a mainframe. This began Project Gutenberg, a library of free ebooks.
events.why: It started the idea that books could be plain data, ready for a reader to display.

events.title: Gyricon: a sheet of twisting balls
events.text: Nick Sheridon joined Xerox PARC in 1975. He came up with a sheet of tiny two-colour balls that turn in an electric field to show black or white. It is often called the first electronic paper. Sources place the idea in the mid-1970s.
events.why: It was the first electric paper: a reflective sheet that held its picture.

events.title: Xerox moves Sheridon off e-paper
events.text: Xerox pulled Sheridon away from electronic paper research in 1977. He returned to it in the mid-1990s.
events.why: The idea waited almost twenty years for the market and the electronics to catch up.

events.title: MIT files the first of two patents behind E Ink
events.text: MIT filed a patent naming Joseph Jacobson and Barrett Comiskey on 25 October 1996. Wikipedia lists a second MIT patent from March 1997. Both were assigned to MIT.
events.why: The lab work behind E Ink began to be protected.

events.title: A particle moves inside a capsule
events.text: Two MIT undergraduates, Barrett Comiskey and JD Albert, working with professor Joseph Jacobson, showed for the first time that an outside electric field could move a particle inside a capsule. Experts had doubted the idea. It happened at about 2 or 3 in the morning in a windowless basement lab.
events.why: It proved the capsule could be a pixel.

events.title: E Ink Corporation is founded
events.who: Jacobson, Albert, Comiskey, Jerome Rubin, Russ Wilcox
events.text: E Ink was founded in 1997 by Jacobson, Albert, Comiskey, Jerome Rubin and Russ Wilcox, according to Wikipedia. It was set up about two months before Albert and Comiskey graduated. Its aim was to turn the lab result into a product.
events.why: A lab trick became something a factory could make.

events.title: The Nature paper
events.text: The team described their electrophoretic ink for printed, reflective displays in the journal Nature. The authors were Comiskey, Albert, Yoshizawa and Jacobson.
events.why: It put the capsule ink on the scientific record.

events.title: The Rocket eBook goes on sale
events.who: Martin Eberhard and Marc Tarpenning, NuvoMedia
events.text: NuvoMedia launched the Rocket eBook at $499. It held about ten books and had an LCD screen with two page-turn buttons, not e-ink. About 20,000 sold in 1999.
events.why: It showed people would read books on a device, and also how much better a paper-like screen would be.

events.title: E Ink's first product: a shop sign
events.text: E Ink introduced its first product, an in-store display sign, for the department store J.C. Penney.
events.why: Shop signs were the first place a screen that holds its picture could pay off.

events.title: Gemstar buys the Rocket's maker
events.text: Gemstar-TV Guide bought NuvoMedia for $187 million and merged it with SoftBook to make the RCA eBook Reader.
events.why: The first ebook readers were a business before the right screen existed.

events.title: Sony Librie: the first e-ink reader
events.text: Sony released the Librie in Japan, an e-book reader with an E Ink display, widely described as the first. The 6-inch screen was 600 by 800 pixels at 170 dots per inch.
events.why: A paper-like screen met a book-shaped device.

events.title: Philips sells its e-paper business
events.text: Philips sold its electronic paper business and patents to Prime View International in 2005. Xerox closed its Gyricon subsidiary that December, reportedly because it could not find backplanes below about $10 per square foot.
events.why: Cost, not the physics, decided which e-paper survived.

events.title: Sony Reader reaches the USA
events.text: Sony launched the PRS-500 Reader in the USA in 2006. It showed 4 levels of grey.
events.why: E-readers left Japan.

events.title: A sunlight-readable screen for a $100 laptop
events.text: Mary Lou Jepsen, chief technology officer and hardware designer of One Laptop per Child, led work on the XO-1 screen. It showed colour with a backlight indoors and switched to black and white in sunlight. It was not e-ink, but it also relied on reflecting daylight.
events.why: It showed the power of reflecting light instead of fighting the sun.

events.title: The first Kindle
events.text: Amazon released the first Kindle at $399. Its 600 by 800 pixel screen, at 167 dots per inch, showed 4 levels of grey.
events.why: It made e-ink a mass market product.

events.title: A magazine cover that changes
events.text: Esquire magazine's October 2008 issue was the first to integrate E Ink into its cover.
events.why: E-ink moved off the reader and onto paper.

events.title: Kindle 2 quadruples the greys
events.text: The Kindle 2 had 16 levels of grey on the same 600 by 800 screen, up from 4.
events.why: More greys made photos and anti-aliased text look better.

events.title: Prime View completes its purchase of E Ink
events.text: Prime View agreed in June 2008 to buy E Ink for $215 million, later raised to $450 million. The sale closed on 24 December 2009, and the buyer renamed itself E Ink Holdings.
events.why: The ink's inventor and its biggest maker became one company.

events.title: Triton: 16 greys and 4,096 colours
events.text: E Ink announced Triton, a display that shows 16 shades of grey and 4,096 colours through a colour filter. Colour e-readers using it came later.
events.why: Colour arrived, at the price of sharpness.

events.title: Kindle Paperwhite adds a frontlight
events.text: Amazon announced the Paperwhite with a 212 dots per inch screen, 62% more pixels than before, and a built-in LED frontlight. It shipped on 1 October. It has 768 by 1024 pixels and 16 greys.
events.why: Readers could now be used in bed without a lamp.

events.title: Carta: sharper pages
events.text: E Ink announced Carta, with 768 by 1024 pixels and 212 dots per inch on 6-inch screens.
events.why: Text started to look like print.

events.title: E-ink inventors enter the Hall of Fame
events.who: JD Albert, Barrett Comiskey and Joseph Jacobson
events.text: Joseph Jacobson, JD Albert and Barrett Comiskey were inducted into the US National Inventors Hall of Fame for electronic ink. That same month E Ink announced Advanced Color ePaper, which uses four pigments.
events.why: The undergraduates' basement experiment was recognised as an invention.

events.title: Kaleido colour e-paper announced
events.text: In December 2019 E Ink announced a colour technology called Print Color. E Ink says the first Kaleido product launched in Q2 2020, and Kaleido Plus followed in March 2021. Wikipedia lists Kaleido 3 in 2023.
events.why: Colour became a normal option on reading tablets.

events.title: Colour e-ink phones
events.text: Hisense released the A5C and A5 Pro in 2020, described as the first colour e-ink smartphones.
events.why: E-paper moved from readers to the thing in your pocket.

events.title: Kindle Colorsoft
events.text: The Colorsoft Signature Edition has a 7-inch screen, with 300 pixels per inch in black and white and 150 in colour, and a frontlight. It was announced in October 2024 at $279.99.
events.why: It shows the colour trade-off in one spec sheet.

series.title: How sharp e-reader screens became
series.caption: From 170 pixels per inch on the first reader to 300 in black and white on a modern one.

points.label: Kindle Colorsoft: 300 ppi black and white

series.title: Shades of grey on e-readers
series.caption: Four shades in 2006 and 2007, sixteen from 2009 on.

facts: The microcapsule breakthrough came on 23 January 1997, at about 2 or 3 in the morning, in a windowless basement lab.
E Ink was founded two months before its two student inventors graduated.
Xerox closed its e-paper subsidiary in 2005, reportedly over the cost of the transistor backplane, not the ink.
The Rocket eBook of 1998 had an LCD, not e-ink, and held about ten books.
